strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use feasible population-based differential evolution (DE) to search the supplied discretization directly. Every individual is a complete h vector; mutation and crossover change multiple coordinates at once, and a joint capped-simplex projection restores both the box and mass constraints before scoring. Rank and select candidates using the exact finite-support correlation objective, without gradients, smoothing, or an approximate score.

This is materially different from the earlier local approaches: it uses neither smooth-maximum continuation with SLSQP, an affine trust-region LP, nor one-coordinate-pair searches. DE maintains several candidates and explores through differences between population members, which is a plausible way to explore distinct basins and handle switches between worst lags. The correlation formula, feasibility set, projection, and selection scores are exact. The population search and its mutation settings are heuristics: they do not guarantee improvement, attainment of 0.3808, or a global optimum. Projection can also bias proposals near box faces. Preserve the repaired parent throughout so that an unsuccessful search cannot lose the available construction.

2. Mathematical specification
Let N be the runtime number of samples, d = 2/N, and M = N/2. A feasible vector h in R^N satisfies 0 <= h_i <= 1 and sum_i h_i = M, equivalently d sum_i h_i = 1. Keep the supplied parent resolution unchanged; if there is no usable parent, use the optional runtime n_points value or the default specified below.

For every integer lag q from -(N-1) through N-1, define J_q = {j : 0 <= j < N and 0 <= j+q < N}, and define R_q(h) = d sum over j in J_q of h[j+q] * (1-h[j]). The exact objective is C(h) = max_q R_q(h). In increasing-q order these values are exactly np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full') * d. Include q=0 and both lag directions. Each lag uses only its finite overlap J_q; do not use circular correlation or replace this objective with an autocorrelation identity that omits boundary terms.

For a finite proposal v, the Euclidean projection onto the feasible capped simplex is P(v)_i = clip(v_i-lambda, 0, 1), where lambda is chosen so that sum_i P(v)_i = M. This follows from the KKT conditions for minimizing one-half of the squared distance to v under the box and sum constraints. Determine lambda by bisection and repair only the resulting small mass residual within available box capacity, as specified in section 3. Do not clip and then rescale.

For a feasible DE population x_0,...,x_(P-1), a rand/1 donor for target i is v = x_r1 + F(x_r2-x_r3), with r1,r2,r3 distinct and different from i. A current-to-best/1 donor is v = x_i + F(x_best-x_i) + F(x_r1-x_r2), with r1 and r2 distinct and different from i. Every population member and x_best has mass M, so each donor also has mass M before crossover in exact arithmetic. Binomial crossover selects donor coordinates with probability CR and keeps the other target coordinates; because crossover generally changes the mass, project the crossed vector with P before scoring. Donors need not satisfy the box constraints; the projection enforces them.

3. Implementation procedure
1. Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) at top level and put every helper at top level as well. Use NumPy and math; no filesystem or network I/O, printing, closures, or lambdas. The generated program performs all input validation, search, exact scoring, and fallback selection. It need not call the pre-imported evaluator.

2. Resolve the parent and N at runtime. Read initial_h_values from globals without redefining, serializing, or hard-coding it. Attempt float64 conversion and accept it as a usable parent only if it is one-dimensional, has at least two entries, all entries are finite, and max(abs(entry)) <= 1e6. If accepted, set N to its length regardless of kwargs['n_points']; make a local working copy and use the parent as the first candidate. Do not resample it. If absent or unusable, parse kwargs.get('n_points') as a finite integer-valued scalar; if that fails use N=95, then clamp N to [2,999]. For seed, accept a finite integer-valued value, reduce it modulo 2^32, and create np.random.default_rng from it; use 42 if conversion or validation fails.

3. Implement a top-level capped-simplex projection helper taking a one-dimensional vector v, N, and M. Reject wrong shape, nonfinite values, or max(abs(v)) > 1e6. Set the bisection endpoints to lo=min(v)-1 and hi=max(v); at lo the clipped sum is N and at hi it is zero. Run 80 iterations. At each midpoint compute clip(v-midpoint, 0, 1); if its sum exceeds M, set lo to the midpoint, otherwise set hi to the midpoint. Form y using the final midpoint. Let delta=M-sum(y). If delta is positive, visit coordinates in order and add min(delta, 1-y[i]); if delta is negative, visit coordinates in order and subtract min(-delta, y[i]). Recompute the residual and make at most two passes, stopping when its magnitude is at most 1e-12*max(1,N). Return failure unless y is finite, every entry is in [0,1], and abs(sum(y)-M) <= 1e-9*max(1,N). Use this same helper for parent repair, initial profiles, DE trials, and restart profiles.

4. Implement a top-level feasibility checker requiring a one-dimensional finite float64 vector of length N, entries in [0,1], and mass error at most 1e-9*max(1,N). Implement a separate exact-score helper that rejects malformed or nonfinite vectors and otherwise returns float(max(np.correlate(h, 1.0-h, mode='full')) * (2.0/N)). Catch numerical exceptions and return positive infinity for an invalid score. Use this exact helper for every population ranking, incumbent comparison, and final score; never use a DE donor or other surrogate value as a score.

5. Establish an immutable feasible fallback before constructing the population. If the parent is usable, project its local copy and use the result as the fallback and first individual. Otherwise use a float64 vector filled with 0.5. Compute its exact score and initialize a separate global incumbent from it. The fallback is never overwritten. Replace the global incumbent only when a feasible candidate's exact score is lower by more than 1e-12; ties retain the existing incumbent.

6. Construct the initial population algorithmically. Offer, in order, the fallback; the uniform 0.5 vector; two block profiles; six wave profiles; and four perturbations of the fallback. For a block profile, set floor(M) consecutive cyclic coordinates to one, the next coordinate to M-floor(M) if that fraction is nonzero, and all other coordinates to zero; use offsets 0 and floor(N/2). For waves, use 0.5 + 0.22*sin(2*pi*k*i/N + phase), with i=0,...,N-1, k in {1,3,5}, and phase in {0, pi/2}. For the perturbations, draw standard-normal z, subtract its mean, form fallback + sigma*z with sigma in {0.04, 0.10, 0.20, 0.35}, and project. Project every profile before use. Deduplicate projected profiles if their maximum coordinate difference from an existing profile is below 1e-8.

7. Fill the population to its configured size. For each additional member, cycle between a raw vector drawn independently from Uniform[0,1]^N and a centered Gaussian perturbation of the fallback. For the latter, draw standard-normal z, subtract its mean, and use sigma cycling through {0.06, 0.14, 0.28, 0.40}. Project and deduplicate each candidate. Limit duplicate-retry attempts to 20*P; if this limit is reached, append a feasible duplicate rather than fail to construct the population. Set X to the resulting P-by-N float64 array and compute an exact score for each row. Keep the fallback in the population at the first position initially, while also retaining it separately for the whole run.

8. Set search budgets by N: for 2 <= N <= 128 use P=32 and G=120 generations; for 129 <= N <= 256 use P=20 and G=60; for 257 <= N <= 999 use P=12 and G=8. These sizes all permit the distinct DE indices required below. For a supplied parent longer than 999, do not resize it and skip population search; return its projected fallback after exact scoring. When search is skipped, still execute final feasibility checks and compute the exact full-correlation score.

9. Run generations synchronously. At the start of each generation, make a snapshot of X and its scores, and snapshot the global best for use in all current-to-best mutations in that generation. For each target i, draw F uniformly from [0.45,0.85] and CR uniformly from [0.65,0.95]. With probability 0.7 use rand/1: choose three distinct population indices other than i and form the donor in section 2. Otherwise use current-to-best/1: choose two distinct indices other than i and form its donor using the generation-start global-best snapshot. For crossover, independently select each coordinate from the donor with probability CR, use the target value otherwise, and force one uniformly chosen coordinate to come from the donor. Project the resulting trial with the capped-simplex helper. If projection fails, the trial is infeasible, or its maximum coordinate difference from the target is below 1e-14, skip it. Otherwise compute its exact score; ignore nonfinite scores.

10. Use elitist target selection: replace target i in the next-generation copy only if the trial score is less than its snapshot target score by more than 1e-12. Independently compare every finite feasible trial with the global incumbent and update that incumbent only on an exact-score improvement greater than 1e-12. Build all trials from the generation snapshot, not from partially updated population members. After all targets have been processed, replace X and its scores with the completed next generation. Count a generation as stagnant if no trial improved the global incumbent by more than 1e-12; otherwise reset the stagnation counter to zero.

11. Implement a deterministic population restart after 20 consecutive stagnant generations, at most twice and only if generations remain. Keep the global best as the first restart member. Add the best distinct members of the current population in stable score order until the elite count E=max(4, floor(P/4)) is reached; if there are too few distinct members, fill the remaining elite slots with feasible duplicates. Fill the rest of the population in slot order. For every fourth non-elite slot, draw a Uniform[0,1]^N vector. For other slots, draw standard-normal z, subtract its mean, and form global_best + sigma*z with sigma cycling through {0.05, 0.12, 0.25, 0.40}. Project each candidate; retry a duplicate or failed proposal up to eight times, then use the last feasible proposal or a duplicate of the fallback. Compute exact scores for new members and update the global incumbent by the same strict rule. Reset stagnation to zero after restarting. Restarts replace members within the fixed G-generation budget; they do not add unbounded work.

12. At termination, project the global incumbent again, check its shape, finiteness, bounds, and mass, and recompute its exact score. Also retain the projected fallback as a final alternative and compare the two final feasible vectors by exact score, so rounding in final projection cannot discard the fallback. If the incumbent cannot be validated, use the fallback; if that also fails validation, use uniform 0.5 at the same N. Return the best valid final vector as float64 h_values, its recomputed Python-float exact score as c5_bound, and integer n_points=N.

4. Search choices and useful variations
The defaults are native parent resolution, P and G as specified in section 3, a 70/30 rand/1 versus current-to-best/1 mixture, F uniform on [0.45,0.85], CR uniform on [0.65,0.95], and up to two restarts after 20 stagnant generations. They require no preliminary tuning. These budgets keep the supplied N=95 case comparatively inexpensive while reducing repeated correlation work for larger arrays.

Correctness requirements do not vary: preserve a usable parent as the fallback, do not change its resolution, use all 2N-1 finite-support lags through the exact full np.correlate formula, enforce box and mass jointly, and accept candidates only from exact-score comparisons. Do not use circular correlation or describe DE as a global optimizer.

A coder may choose a population size in roughly [16,48], adjust generations within about [40,160] for N<=128, vary F within [0.3,0.95], CR within [0.5,1.0], change the rand/1 mixture probability within [0.5,0.85], or vary the Gaussian start scales within [0.03,0.45]. The specified defaults are the usable choice if no variation is made. Any result-dependent adaptation must remain explicit in the program; the default is the fixed stagnation counter and capped restart rule above. Larger N should retain a smaller finite budget or skip search rather than silently resample the parent.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
Use float64 throughout. The capped-simplex projection is the joint feasibility mechanism; do not clip and rescale successively. Check all runtime inputs and all generated candidates for shape and finiteness before use. The projection checks bounds and mass after its residual repair. A failed projection, nonfinite exact score, or exception in one trial leaves its target and the global incumbent unchanged. If population creation or search raises an exception, preserve the already established fallback and incumbent.

For feasible h, every product h[j+q]*(1-h[j]) is bounded, so the exact correlation scores are finite and small; the exact scorer still checks finiteness and catches errors. At N=95, a population of 32 stores only 3,040 float64 values, and each exact full correlation has 189 outputs. Memory is O(PN) plus one O(N) correlation result; do not construct a dense Jacobian, Hessian, or pairwise quadratic tensor. Build one generation at a time and run it serially on the available single CPU. For N<=128 the default search uses at most P*G trial scores plus initialization and at most two bounded restart fills. The reduced budgets through N=999 limit the cost of direct np.correlate; above 999, preserve and score the parent without evolutionary search. Fixed generation counts, retry limits, bisection iterations, and restart counts bound program work.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
All parent validation, feasibility restoration, population construction, random search, candidate evaluation, acceptance, and fallback selection must be source-code operations executed by the harness later. Do not rely on the pre-imported evaluator for the score and do not claim that a score has been measured. Read the pre-imported initial_h_values if usable; never redefine or serialize its entries. Catch conversion, projection, and per-candidate scoring failures locally so they cannot erase a valid fallback.

Immediately before returning, require a one-dimensional finite vector of length N, every entry in [0,1], and abs(sum(h)-N/2) <= 1e-9*max(1,N). If the best candidate fails, select the validated projected fallback, then uniform 0.5 as the final feasibility fallback. Compute c5_bound from the exact returned vector using max(np.correlate(h, 1-h, mode='full')) * (2.0/N), including every lag. If exact scoring raises even for the selected fallback, return the scorer's positive-infinity failure sentinel rather than fabricating a score. Return exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values float64 and one-dimensional, c5_bound a Python float, and n_points the matching integer length. The program must return its best exact-score feasible candidate and must not claim that the target bound has been attained.
